research.notes: INSTALL FOR THIS LANE ON THIS RIG (RTX 5090 / sm_120 / Win11): The constrained-decoding library is NOT a GPU concern — every engine here is a CPU-side logits processor (an Earley/FSM parser computes a token bitmask each step on the CPU). Blackwell-readiness therefore flows entirely from the INFERENCE engine, not the grammar lib. So: pick your serving engine first (from the inference-server lane), then bolt on the matching grammar backend. Concrete stack for this rig: (1) `pip install xgrammar` (Apache-2.0, ships a native Win x86-64 cp3.9-3.14 wheel, XGrammar-2 v0.2.1) — it is the DEFAULT structured-output backend baked into vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and MLC-LLM, so on a native-Windows vLLM build you get it for free with `guided_json`/`structural_tag`; <40us/token, 6-80x faster grammar compile than v1, and Structural Tag is the right primitive for reliable tool-calls. (2) For pure-local llama.cpp / Ollama work, use the built-in GBNF grammar + `format:` JSON-schema knobs — zero install, fully Windows-native, no extra dependency, and llama.cpp auto-converts JSON-schema -> GBNF in llama-server's OpenAI `response_format`. (3) Add `pip install instructor pydantic` (MIT, v1.15.1) as the application-layer wrapper for your LLM-crew: it does NOT constrain tokens (it is retry+Pydantic-validate around any provider, incl. local Ollama), so it composes cleanly ON TOP of (1)/(2) and gives type-safe Python objects with automatic re-ask on validation failure. THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT TAKEAWAY: constrained decoding makes a *grammatically* valid artifact, never a *semantically correct* one — a 100%-valid-JSON tool-call can still call the wrong tool with wrong args. That maps directly onto the workflow EXTERNAL_VERIFIER standard: the grammar layer is the deterministic floor (XGrammar/GBNF guarantees the shape), Instructor's Pydantic validators are the cheap second check (constraints/enums/ranges), and a different-family model verifies semantics on top. Two known landmines on this rig, both library-agnostic because they live in the engine: native-Windows vLLM/SGLang are community-maintained patched builds (devnen/aivrar) not first-party — pin them; and under WSL2, Blackwell FP8 tensor cores are still hidden by dxgkrnl (prefer INT4-AWQ-Marlin there, per waves 1-2). XGrammar-2's compile speedup is the thing that actually matters for an agent crew doing many short distinct tool-call grammars (cross-grammar cache + JIT), so prefer it over Outlines/llguidance backends for tool-calling fan-out specifically.

engines.summary: The constrained-decoding capability built directly into the llama.cpp runtime you already use for local GGUF inference — no extra package, fully Windows-native, the local-first default for this rig. For raw non-JSON DSLs (custom game-data formats, enum menus, restricted dialogue) hand-authored GBNF is the most direct tool in the lane. GPU side follows the wave-1/2 rules (cu128 build, CUDA graphs, never eager); the grammar layer is orthogonal to those.

(2) Pin the grammar lib explicitly so it doesn't drift: `pip install "xgrammar==0.2.1"`. (3) Launch: `python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --model Qwen/Qwen3-14B-AWQ --quantization awq_marlin --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --max-model-len 16384 --guided-decoding-backend xgrammar` (AWQ-Marlin per wave-1/2; never --enforce-eager — CUDA graphs ~8x). (4) Call structured output: POST /v1/chat/completions with `"response_format": {"type":"json_schema","json_schema":{...}}` or `"guided_json": <schema>`. For tool-calls use vLLM's tool API (XGrammar Structural Tag enforces the harmony/tool shape). VRAM: Qwen3-14B-AWQ ~9-10GB leaves headroom on 32GB for long context + KV cache.

extras.name: llama-cpp-gbnf-json-schema-local-windows
extras.note: GOAL: zero-Python-dependency, fully-Windows-native structured JSON from a GGUF model — the local-first default that needs no extra install beyond llama.cpp itself. (1) Build/grab a cu128 llama.cpp (wave-1/2: CUDA 12.8, NOT 13.x — 13.x segfaults MMQ + ~5x slower). (2) Start the server: `llama-server -m model.gguf -ngl 99 -c 16384 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080` (-ngl 99 offloads all layers to the 5090; CUDA graphs on by default). (3) Constrain via OpenAI-compatible response_format — POST /v1/chat/completions with `"response_format":{"type":"json_schema","json_schema":{"schema":{...}}}`; llama-server auto-converts the schema to GBNF. (4) For a custom non-JSON grammar, pass `"grammar": "root ::=..."` (raw GBNF) instead. CAVEAT: the JSON-schema->GBNF converter supports only a SUBSET (no full $ref/if-then-else) and the schema is NOT injected into the prompt — describe the expected shape in your system prompt too, or the model fills valid-but-wrong values.

extras.name: ollama-format-jsonschema-plus-instructor
extras.note: GOAL: easiest local structured artifacts for the LLM-crew on Windows — Ollama (native Windows installer, no WSL) for constrained decoding + Instructor for typed Pydantic objects and retries. (1) `winget install Ollama.Ollama` then `ollama pull qwen3:14b`. (2) Constrain at the source by passing a JSON-schema to Ollama's `format` field. (3) Wrap with Instructor for type safety + auto-retry: `pip install "instructor>=1.15.1" pydantic`; then `import instructor; from openai import OpenAI; client = instructor.from_openai(OpenAI(base_url='http://localhost:11434/v1', api_key='ollama'), mode=instructor.Mode.JSON); obj = client.chat.completions.create(model='qwen3:14b', response_model=MyPydanticModel, messages=[...], max_retries=3)`. Ollama's `format` makes attempt-1 already schema-shaped; Instructor's Pydantic validators catch field-level invariants (enums/ranges/cross-field) that grammars cannot express and re-ask on failure. This is the deterministic-floor + cheap-validator combo from the workflow standards.

extras.name: outlines-multibackend-python-rtx5090
extras.note: GOAL: one Python API for structured generation across local backends without rewriting per engine (good for the crew's Python tooling). (1) `pip install "outlines>=1.3.0"` (pulls outlines-core 0.2.14 Rust wheel — installs clean on Windows). (2) Against local llama.cpp: `import outlines; from outlines import models, generate; model = models.llamacpp('model.gguf', n_gpu_layers=99)` then `gen = generate.json(model, MyPydanticModel); result = gen(prompt)` — returns a validated instance. (3) Regex-constrained field: `generate.regex(model, r'\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}')`. (4) Against a vLLM server use the vLLM backend, or against Ollama use the Ollama backend — same generate.json call. (5) v1.2.10+ adds LM Studio (MLX) backend, but MLX is Apple-only REFERENCE — not relevant on this rig. Use Outlines when you want backend-portability; use XGrammar-in-the-engine when raw tool-calling throughput matters.

extras.name: sglang-grammar-backend-switch-blackwell-wsl2
extras.note: GOAL: pick the right grammar backend in SGLang (no native-Windows SGLang build exists — this path is WSL2). WSL2 NOTE (wave-1/2): WSL2 2.7.0 finally enables CUDA-graph capture on sm_120 (run `nvidia-cdi-refresh` after driver updates), but Blackwell FP8 tensor cores are STILL hidden by dxgkrnl — so prefer INT4-AWQ-Marlin weights here, not FP8. Launch with default (XGrammar): `python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-14B-AWQ --quantization awq_marlin --grammar-backend xgrammar`. Switch only if XGrammar hits a schema edge case: `--grammar-backend llguidance` (full EBNF + fastest TTFT, ~50us/token) or `--grammar-backend outlines` (JSON-schema + regex, no EBNF). Backend support matrix: XGrammar = JSON-schema + regex + EBNF (default, best fan-out throughput via cross-grammar cache); llguidance = JSON-schema + regex + EBNF (best TTFT, dynamic grammars); outlines = JSON-schema + regex only.

extras.name: guidance-templated-generation-local-windows
extras.note: GOAL: multi-step templated generation (interleave fixed text + select() menus + constrained slots) on a local model, Windows-native. (1) `pip install "guidance>=0.3.2"` (pulls the llguidance Rust engine; pure-Python front end installs on Windows). (2) Load a local backend: `from guidance import models, gen, select; lm = models.LlamaCpp('model.gguf', n_gpu_layers=99)`. (3) Build a program: `lm += f'Classify sentiment: {text}\nSentiment: ' + select(['positive','negative','neutral'], name='label')` then read `lm['label']` — guaranteed one of the options. (4) Constrained slot: `lm += 'Year: ' + gen(regex=r'\d{4}', name='year')`. 2026 builds add speculative execution (~2x). USE THIS over XGrammar when you want the program-as-template paradigm (menus, token-healing, control flow woven into generation); use XGrammar-in-the-engine for plain single-shot guided_json/tool-calls (simpler + faster there).

extras.name: verifier-stack-grammar-floor-plus-semantic-check
extras.note: GOAL: enforce the EXTERNAL_VERIFIER + UNCERTAINTY_GATED workflow standards for the LLM-crew's tool-calls — because constrained decoding guarantees SHAPE, never CORRECTNESS (valid JSON can still call the wrong tool with wrong args). THREE LAYERS: (1) Deterministic floor = XGrammar guided_json/Structural Tag (vLLM/SGLang) OR llama.cpp GBNF — output is grammatically valid by construction, no model can violate the schema. (2) Cheap structural validator = Instructor Pydantic model with field_validator (enums, numeric ranges, cross-field invariants, referential checks against your game's registries) — catches semantically-broken-but-grammatically-valid output and auto-re-asks with the error (max_retries=3). (3) Semantic verifier = a DIFFERENT model family (e.g. if the generator is Qwen, verify with a Llama/Gemma) judging whether the tool-call actually accomplishes the intent, with the generator's reasoning HIDDEN (Kambhampati arXiv:2402.01817 — no model verifies its own output). Gate a human checkpoint on layer-3 disagreement, not on every call. This is the floor+ceiling+verifier pattern, not grammar-alone.

extras.name: squeezebits-guided-decoding-benchmark-reference
extras.note: REFERENCE: measured guided-decoding throughput/latency comparison of XGrammar vs Outlines vs llguidance backends across vLLM and SGLang. Use to sanity-check backend choice before committing the crew's pipeline. Headline: XGrammar is the default and generally wins per-token latency for reused grammars (caching); llguidance wins time-to-first-token on complex/one-off grammars. Numbers are H100-class but the RELATIVE backend ordering holds on the 5090 since the mask compute is CPU-side.

research.domain: Local speech inference runtimes — ASR (speech-to-text) and TTS (text-to-speech) engine layer for game voiceover + audio production. Catalogues the engines that RUN speech models, not the models. Filtered for HP OMEN 45L · RTX 5090 (Blackwell sm_120, 32 GB VRAM) · Core Ultra 9 · 64 GB RAM · Windows 11 Pro · CUDA 12.8+.
research.notes:
WHAT TO INSTALL ON THIS RIG, by job: ASR (transcription / subtitle alignment / voice-command dev):
1. whisper.cpp v1.8.6 — the no-drama default. Native Windows + CUDA (cuBLAS + custom kernels), GGML/GGUF models, builds clean for sm_120 with `-DGGML_CUDA=1 -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120` on CUDA 12.8. Zero Python, zero PyTorch, no Blackwell pain. This is the one to reach for first for bulk transcription and offline subtitle generation.
2. faster-whisper 1.2.1 (CTranslate2 4.7.2) — fastest batched throughput AND lowest-friction Python ASR. THE BLACKWELL CATCH (load-bearing): the default `int8_float16` compute type crashes on the 5090 with CUBLAS_STATUS_NOT_SUPPORTED (CTranslate2 INT8-tensor-core padding bug; fix PR #1982 merged but the 4.7.2 pip wheel does NOT yet advertise sm_120). RUN WITH `compute_type="float16"` — it works perfectly and is plenty fast on a 5090. Pair cuDNN 9 + cuBLAS for CUDA 12. Use this for word-aligned, batched, or programmatic transcription.
3. sherpa-onnx 1.13.2 — the Swiss-army runtime: ASR + TTS + VAD + diarization in ONE C++/ONNXRuntime engine, true streaming, runs Parakeet/Whisper/Kokoro/Piper-style models, ships prebuilt Windows CUDA 12.x binaries AND a DirectML provider (no CUDA toolchain needed). The integration backbone if you want one engine for both live ASR and TTS in-engine (Godot/UE5). TTS (game voiceover / NPC barks / narration):
4. Piper (OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl, GPLv3) — instant, tiny ONNX neural TTS, hundreds of voices, real-time on CPU alone; the workhorse for high-volume placeholder/NPC VO. GPLv3 — keep it as a separate process, don't statically link into proprietary game code. CPU is fine here; GPU buys little.
5. Kokoro (82M) via sherpa-onnx or kokoro-onnx (Apache-2.0) — #1 on TTS Arena Jan 2026, ~36x real-time on GPU, <2 GB VRAM, fully commercial-OK. Best quality-per-byte for shippable English VO.
6. XTTS-v2 (coqui-tts fork, Idiap) for zero-shot voice cloning from a 6-sec sample, <200ms streaming — but the weights are Coqui Public Model License (NON-COMMERCIAL): great for previz/temp VO, NOT for shipping a game. Use Kokoro/Piper for anything you ship. THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT TAKEAWAY: On Blackwell sm_120, the C/C++ ONNX/GGML engines (whisper.cpp, sherpa-onnx, Piper, Kokoro-ONNX) are the happy path — native Windows, no PyTorch, no sm_120 wheel roulette. The PyTorch-based stack (WhisperX, NeMo/Parakeet, XTTS, Kyutai) inherits the whole-ecosystem Blackwell tax: you need cu128 nightlies and often a `get_device_capability()→(9,0)` Hopper spoof to stop nvrtc crashing on sm_120/sm_121, and NVIDIA Riva/NIM is WSL2-only (which hides FP8/FP4 tensor cores). For faster-whisper specifically, the one rule that saves you is: never use the default int8 compute type on this card — set float16.

engines.summary: The no-drama ASR default for this rig. Pure C/C++ port of Whisper on ggml — builds natively on Windows with `cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=1` and runs large-v3 entirely on the 5090 via cuBLAS + custom CUDA kernels, with no PyTorch, no CTranslate2, and therefore none of the sm_120 wheel roulette that plagues the Python ASR stack. Consumes GGML/GGUF model files (quantized q5/q8 variants available to shrink VRAM further). Ships a `whisper-server` (OpenAI-compatible endpoint), CLI, and bindings. Vulkan backend gives a vendor-neutral fallback. The trade-off vs faster-whisper is no batched multi-stream throughput, so for bulk parallel transcription faster-whisper wins — but for reliability-first single-stream offline transcription and live capture on Windows, this is the engine to start with.

extras.name: whisper-cpp-windows-cuda-sm120-build
extras.note:
Build whisper.cpp v1.8.6 from source for RTX 5090 (sm_120) on Windows 11 with CUDA 12.8 — the no-PyTorch ASR path. Prereqs: Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools (C++ workload), CUDA Toolkit 12.8, CMake. Commands (PowerShell): git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp; cd whisper.cpp cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=1 -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=1 cmake --build build -j --config Release
Download a model:.\models\download-ggml-model.cmd large-v3-turbo
Transcribe:.\build\bin\Release\whisper-cli.exe -m models\ggml-large-v3-turbo.bin -f audio.wav -of out -otxt -osrt
Notes: -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 is the load-bearing flag for Blackwell. Use CUDA 12.8 NOT 13.x (wave-1 lesson: 13.x is ~5x slower / segfaults MMQ in llama.cpp; same ggml backend here). -osrt emits SubRip subtitles. For a server:.\build\bin\Release\whisper-server.exe -m models\ggml-large-v3-turbo.bin --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 (OpenAI-compatible /inference endpoint).

extras.name: faster-whisper-blackwell-float16-fix
extras.note:
Install + run faster-whisper on the RTX 5090 WITHOUT the int8 cuBLAS crash. Create a venv (Python 3.11), then: pip install faster-whisper==1.2.1 pip install nvidia-cublas-cu12 nvidia-cudnn-cu12==9.* # cuDNN 9 + cuBLAS for CUDA 12
MINIMAL working script — the float16 line is mandatory on Blackwell: from faster_whisper import WhisperModel model = WhisperModel('large-v3', device='cuda', compute_type='float16') # NOT the default int8_float16 — that throws CUBLAS_STATUS_NOT_SUPPORTED on sm_120 segments, info = model.transcribe('audio.wav', beam_size=5, vad_filter=True, word_timestamps=True) for s in segments: print(f'[{s.start:.2f}->{s.end:.2f}] {s.text}')
Batched (4x faster) for bulk corpora: from faster_whisper import BatchedInferencePipeline bp = BatchedInferencePipeline(model=model); bp.transcribe('audio.wav', batch_size=16)
Why: CTranslate2 4.7.2's INT8 tensor-core path lacks sm_120 padding (fix PR #1982 merged but not in the advertised wheel). float16 sidesteps it and is fast on a 5090; INT8's VRAM savings are irrelevant at 32 GB. Set HF_HUB_DISABLE_SYMLINKS_WARNING=1 on Windows to silence cache warnings.

extras.name: sherpa-onnx-windows-cuda-prebuilt-asr-tts
extras.note:
Get a unified ASR+TTS engine on Windows with ZERO compilation, using sherpa-onnx 1.13.2 prebuilt CUDA 12.x binaries. Python path (simplest): pip install sherpa-onnx # CPU build; for CUDA on Windows download the prebuilt GPU package from the releases page (sherpa-onnx-vX.X.X-win-x64-cuda.tar.bz2) OR use the C++ libs directly
ASR (Parakeet/Whisper ONNX) — download a model dir, then: sherpa-onnx-offline --tokens=tokens.txt --whisper-encoder=enc.onnx --whisper-decoder=dec.onnx --provider=cuda audio.wav
TTS (Kokoro, Apache-2.0, shippable): curl -L -O https://github.com/k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx/releases/download/tts-models/kokoro-en-v0_19.tar.bz2 (extract) sherpa-onnx-offline-tts --kokoro-model=model.onnx --kokoro-voices=voices.bin --kokoro-tokens=tokens.txt --kokoro-data-dir=espeak-ng-data --provider=cuda --output-filename=line.wav 'Your dialogue line here.'

extras.name: kokoro-onnx-shippable-tts-gpu
extras.note:
Shippable, license-clean (Apache-2.0 weights + MIT runtime) high-quality TTS on the RTX 5090. Install: pip install kokoro-onnx soundfile pip install onnxruntime-gpu # CUDA EP runs on sm_120 with no PyTorch-wheel issue curl -L -O https://github.com/thewh1teagle/kokoro-onnx/releases/download/model-files-v1.0/kokoro-v1.0.onnx curl -L -O https://github.com/thewh1teagle/kokoro-onnx/releases/download/model-files-v1.0/voices-v1.0.bin
Generate: from kokoro_onnx import Kokoro; import soundfile as sf k = Kokoro('kokoro-v1.0.onnx', 'voices-v1.0.bin') samples, sr = k.create('The relay went silent three hours ago.', voice='af_sarah', speed=1.0, lang='en-us') sf.write('line.wav', samples, sr)
Force GPU EP explicitly: set ONNX provider via import onnxruntime as ort; ort.get_available_providers() — ensure 'CUDAExecutionProvider' is listed. ~36x real-time, <2 GB VRAM, so you can spin many voices concurrently. Use this for final English narration/character VO; it is the commercial-safe quality pick over XTTS (non-commercial) and Piper (lower quality).

extras.name: whisperx-blackwell-diarization-sm120-spoof
extras.note:
Run WhisperX (word timestamps + speaker diarization) on the RTX 5090 despite the sm_120 nvrtc crash. The blocker: torchaudio/pyannote's Jiterator compiler doesn't know sm_120/sm_121 and crashes on complex-FFT.abs(). Fix = pin Blackwell-capable PyTorch + spoof device capability to Hopper (sm_90 binaries run natively on Blackwell). Steps (venv, Python 3.11): pip install torch torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 # cu128 nightly — NOT stable cu121/cu124 (no sm_120 kernels) pip install whisperx
Apply the capability spoof at the TOP of your script BEFORE importing whisperx/torchaudio: import torch; _orig = torch.cuda.get_device_capability torch.cuda.get_device_capability = lambda *a, **k: (9, 0) # report Hopper; sm_90 PTX/cubin runs on sm_120 via binary compat
Then: import whisperx m = whisperx.load_model('large-v3', 'cuda', compute_type='float16') # float16 (faster-whisper int8 also crashes on sm_120) result = m.transcribe('audio.wav', batch_size=16) # alignment + diarization (needs HF token for pyannote, accept model terms): model_a, meta = whisperx.load_align_model(language_code=result['language'], device='cuda') result = whisperx.align(result['segments'], model_a, meta, 'audio.wav', 'cuda')
Or just clone the Mekopa/whisperx-blackwell fork which bakes in the spoof + jiterator bypass. If you DON'T need diarization, skip all this and use plain faster-whisper with compute_type='float16' (recipe above).

extras.name: parakeet-export-to-onnx-for-sherpa
extras.note:
Use NVIDIA's SOTA Parakeet/Canary accuracy WITHOUT the WSL2/Docker/NeMo Blackwell tax — run it as ONNX inside sherpa-onnx natively on Windows. k2-fsa already publishes pre-exported NeMo models; grab one from the releases instead of running NeMo yourself: Browse https://github.com/k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx/releases for 'nemo' / 'parakeet' ONNX bundles (the changelog notes 'NeMo unified streaming 0.6b models exported'). curl -L -O https://github.com/k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx/releases/download/asr-models/sherpa-onnx-nemo-parakeet-<ver>.tar.bz2 (extract)
Offline transcription on GPU: sherpa-onnx-offline --provider=cuda --tokens=tokens.txt --nemo-ctc=model.onnx audio.wav (or --transducer-* for RNNT exports)
Streaming: sherpa-onnx --provider=cuda --tokens=tokens.txt --encoder=enc.onnx --decoder=dec.onnx --joiner=join.onnx (mic or wav)
Why this beats Riva/NIM here: Riva and the NeMo runtime are Windows-via-WSL2-only (which hides the 5090's FP8/FP4 tensor cores) and Docker-gated; the ONNX export runs through ONNXRuntime's CUDA EP natively on sm_120 with no spoof. Only drop to real NeMo (WSL2 + cu128 nightly) if you must FINE-TUNE Parakeet on custom audio.

extras.name: speech-lane-blackwell-survival-card
extras.note: Quick-reference for WHY the speech lane splits into easy/hard paths on this rig, and the fixes. EASY (native Windows, no PyTorch): whisper.cpp, sherpa-onnx, Piper, kokoro-onnx — all ride ggml or ONNXRuntime, both of which target sm_120; just build/run with CUDA 12.8 (whisper.cpp: -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120; ONNX: onnxruntime-gpu, provider=cuda). HARD (PyTorch-based): WhisperX, NeMo/Parakeet, XTTS, Kyutai — stable PyTorch ships only up to sm_90, so on sm_120 you MUST install cu128 nightly wheels (pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128) and often spoof torch.cuda.get_device_capability()->(9,0) so nvrtc emits sm_90 (binary-compatible with Blackwell). TWO recurring crashes + fixes: (1) CTranslate2 int8 -> CUBLAS_STATUS_NOT_SUPPORTED -> use compute_type='float16'. (2) torchaudio complex-FFT Jiterator nvrtc -> capability spoof to (9,0). WSL2 note (wave lesson): WSL2 hides FP8/FP4 tensor cores, so NVIDIA Riva/NIM (WSL2-only on Windows) loses Blackwell's best paths — prefer the native ONNX-export route for Parakeet. NEVER pip install xformers (use SageAttention); never run PyTorch eager where CUDA graphs apply. CUDA 12.8, not 13.x.

research.domain: Profiling, benchmarking & observability for local AI engines (the measurement layer)
research.notes:
INSTALL THIS LANE ON THE 5090 (Windows-native, in order): (1) Live GPU watch -> `pip install nvitop` (NVML-only, no CUDA needed, native Windows). nvitop is the daily driver; gpustat is the scriptable JSON fallback; raw `nvidia-smi dmon -s pucm` is the zero-install floor. (2) Engine throughput truth -> `llama-bench` ships inside every CUDA llama.cpp build you already have (pp512/tg128, JSON out) for GGUF; for OpenAI-compatible servers (vLLM/llama-server/TGI) use `pip install aiperf` (NVIDIA AIPerf 0.8.0 — the supported successor to the now-frozen GenAI-Perf) for TTFT/ITL/throughput, or vLLM's own `vllm bench serve` if vLLM is installed. (3) Kernel/timeline truth -> Nsight Systems 2026.3.1 (timeline, CUDA-graph verification, install the Windows host GUI) + Nsight Compute 2026.2 (per-kernel roofline) — both are native Windows.exe and support GeForce Blackwell sm_120, but you MUST flip NVIDIA Control Panel -> Developer -> Manage GPU Performance Counters -> "Allow access to all users" (or run as admin) or every counter read fails with ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM. (4) Python framework profiling -> torch.profiler (built into PyTorch, exports chrome trace + tensorboard) for training/Diffusers; `pip install py-spy` (0.4.2, native Windows, run terminal as Administrator to attach to a running PID) for "where is my Python stuck" without code changes. (5) LLM-app traces -> `pip install arize-phoenix` (15.1.0, ELv2, fully self-hostable, runs a local UI, OpenTelemetry-native) is the best local-first agent/RAG tracer; instrument with OpenLLMetry (Apache-2.0) for vendor-neutral spans; Langfuse (MIT) if you want prompt-versioning + evals in the same pane.
SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT TAKEAWAY: This rig is Windows-native and DCGM/dcgm-exporter is LINUX-ONLY — there is no native-Windows datacenter telemetry path, so the production Prometheus/Grafana GPU-fleet pattern does NOT apply here; use nvitop/gpustat/nvidia-smi for live VRAM+util and Nsight Systems to PROVE the wave-1/2 config laws (CUDA-graphs ~8x vs eager shows up as kernel-launch gaps collapsing on the timeline; MMQ-path regressions on CUDA 13.x show up as slower GEMM kernels). The Nsight tools are the only way to turn "this recipe is faster" into a measured, screenshot-able fact on the 5090 — and they work on GeForce Blackwell on Windows ONLY after the perf-counter toggle is enabled.

On this rig it catches the failure mode nvitop shows as 'GPU at 0% but the run isn't finished': tokenizer/preprocessing bottlenecks, a blocking data loader, or a CPU-bound sampling loop. Native Windows wheel (0.4.2, 2026-04-24); on Windows you generally need to run the terminal as Administrator to profile a process you didn't launch. Supports CPython through 3.14.

extras.note: ONE-SHOT install of the Windows-native profiling lane on the 5090 (PowerShell, in a venv to avoid polluting global Python). Pin nothing that ships with the driver. `python -m venv E:\AI\tensor_engine\.venv-profiling; E:\AI\tensor_engine\.venv-profiling\Scripts\Activate.ps1; pip install --upgrade pip; pip install nvitop==1.7.0 gpustat py-spy==0.4.2 arize-phoenix==15.1.0 aiperf==0.8.0`. nvidia-smi is already present (driver). Verify: `nvitop -1` (one-shot snapshot) should show the RTX 5090 with 32GB and current VRAM/util.

extras.name: recipe-llama-bench-gguf-flag-sweep-5090
extras.note: Prove a GGUF model's throughput AND find optimal launch flags in one run, using the llama-bench.exe inside your CUDA-12.8 llama.cpp build (NOT a 13.x build — wave-2 law: 13.x segfaults/slows MMQ). From the build dir: `.\llama-bench.exe -m D:\AI-Models\<model>.gguf -p 512 -n 128 -ngl 99 -fa 1 -b 512 --repetitions 5 -o md`. Read pp512 (prefill, compute-bound) and tg128 (decode, bandwidth-bound) with stddev. To SWEEP and pick winners, pass comma lists (cartesian product runs automatically): `.\llama-bench.exe -m D:\AI-Models\<model>.gguf -p 512 -n 128 -ngl 0,99 -fa 0,1 -b 256,512 --repetitions 5 -o csv > E:\AI\tensor_engine\bench-sweep.csv`. On the 5090, -ngl 99 (all layers on GPU) + -fa 1 (flash-attn) should dominate. To catch a CUDA-version regression, run the identical command against a 12.8 build vs a 13.x build and diff pp512. While it runs, in another terminal: `nvidia-smi dmon -s pucm` to confirm the GPU is pinned and VRAM didn't spill.

extras.name: recipe-aiperf-ttft-itl-against-llama-server
extras.note: Measure serving metrics (TTFT/ITL/throughput) of any OpenAI-compatible endpoint on the 5090 with NVIDIA AIPerf 0.8.0 — the supported successor to GenAI-Perf. First start a server (Windows-native llama.cpp is the cleanest 5090 path): `.\llama-server.exe -m D:\AI-Models\<model>.gguf -ngl 99 -fa 1 -c 8192 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080`. Then benchmark (pip-installed aiperf, native Windows or WSL2): `aiperf profile --model <model> --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 --endpoint-type chat --streaming --concurrency 8 --request-count 100`. Report TTFT, ITL, output-token throughput, and request throughput; rerun with --concurrency 1,4,8,16 to draw the latency-vs-throughput knee. Use this (vendor-neutral) instead of `vllm bench` when comparing engines. GenAI-Perf is feature-frozen — do not start new work on it.

extras.name: recipe-vllm-bench-serve-wsl2-int4-awq
extras.note: Benchmark a vLLM server with vLLM's own CLI — ONLY relevant inside WSL2 (vLLM has no native Windows build). Wave-2 law: WSL2 hides the 5090's FP8/FP4 tensor cores, so serve an INT4-AWQ (Marlin) model, not FP8. In WSL2: `vllm serve <org>/<model>-AWQ --quantization awq_marlin --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --max-model-len 8192 &` then `vllm bench serve --model <org>/<model>-AWQ --dataset-name random --num-prompts 200 --request-rate 10 --backend openai --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --percentile-metrics ttft,tpot,itl,e2el --save-result`. Reports TTFT/TPOT/ITL/E2EL + request & output-token throughput. For a vendor-neutral cross-engine number prefer AIPerf instead. Sanity context: vLLM hit ~793 tok/s peak vs Ollama ~41 tok/s in a 2026 head-to-head, so this is the throughput/concurrency path when you commit to WSL2+vLLM.

extras.name: recipe-nsight-systems-prove-cuda-graphs-windows
extras.note: PROVE the CUDA-graphs ~8x law visually on the 5090 with Nsight Systems 2026.3.x (native Windows). FIRST enable counters: NVIDIA Control Panel -> Developer -> Manage GPU Performance Counters -> 'Allow access to the GPU performance counters to all users' (or run the terminal as Administrator) — otherwise GPU metrics fail with ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM. Capture a trace of a llama.cpp run: `nsys profile -t cuda,nvtx,osrt --gpu-metrics-devices=all -o E:\AI\tensor_engine\graphs-on.nsys-rep.\llama-server.exe -m D:\AI-Models\<model>.gguf -ngl 99 -fa 1` (let it serve a few requests, then Ctrl+C). Capture a second trace with CUDA graphs disabled for contrast. Open both.nsys-rep in the Nsight Systems GUI: the eager/graphs-off timeline shows the GPU idle between many tiny kernel launches; graphs-on collapses those gaps into a dense kernel stream — that's the ~8x story made visible. Also check the GPU-metrics row for Tensor-Core activity and DRAM bandwidth during decode. Trace overhead is low; do NOT use Nsight COMPUTE for whole-app timing (it replays kernels — minutes each).

extras.name: recipe-torch-profiler-diffusers-sdxl-trace
extras.note: Profile a Diffusers/ComfyUI SDXL or Flux step (or a local fine-tune) on the 5090 with the built-in torch.profiler and export a chrome trace — no extra install if PyTorch (cu128/cu130) is present. Wrap the hot path: `from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity, schedule` then `with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA], record_shapes=True, profile_memory=True, with_stack=True) as prof:` run a few denoise steps, calling `prof.step()` per iteration; afterwards `prof.export_chrome_trace('E:\\AI\\tensor_engine\\sdxl_trace.json')` and `print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by='cuda_time_total', row_limit=20))`. Open the json in chrome://tracing or Perfetto to see which op dominates CUDA time and whether the GPU stalls on host. For higher-level views (GPU idle %, frequent-kernel patterns, trace-diff between two runs) feed the Kineto trace to Holistic Trace Analysis: `pip install HolisticTraceAnalysis` then `from hta.trace_analysis import TraceAnalysis; TraceAnalysis(trace_dir='E:\\AI\\tensor_engine\\traces').get_gpu_kernel_breakdown()`.

extras.name: recipe-py-spy-unstick-comfyui-on-windows
extras.note: When nvitop shows the GPU at 0% but a Python run (ComfyUI, a tokenizing loop, a data loader) isn't finishing, find the CPU-side culprit WITHOUT restarting it. Run an ELEVATED PowerShell (py-spy needs admin on Windows to attach to a process it didn't launch). Get the PID from nvitop's process panel or `Get-Process python`. Instant stack dump of a hung process: `py-spy dump --pid <PID>`. Live function view: `py-spy top --pid <PID>`. Flame graph of a slow window: `py-spy record --pid <PID> -d 30 -o E:\AI\tensor_engine\flame.svg` (samples ~100 Hz for 30s, negligible overhead). This catches the classic 'GPU idle, pipeline slow' failure mode — a blocking preprocessing/sampling step on the CPU that no GPU profiler will show.

extras.name: recipe-phoenix-local-llm-trace-with-openllmetry
extras.note: Stand up local-first LLM-app observability (traces + evals) on the 5090 box with Arize Phoenix 15.1.0, instrumented vendor-neutrally via OpenLLMetry so traces stay portable. Start the local server (data never leaves the machine): `pip install arize-phoenix==15.1.0; phoenix serve` -> UI at http://localhost:6006. Instrument your app once with the OpenInference/OpenLLMetry auto-instrumentors, e.g. for an OpenAI-compatible local endpoint: `pip install openinference-instrumentation-openai opentelemetry-sdk` then `from phoenix.otel import register; register(project_name='studio-rpg', endpoint='http://localhost:6006/v1/traces', auto_instrument=True)`. Every LLM call (prompt, completion, tokens, latency, tool calls, retrievals) now shows as a trace tree, and you can run built-in LLM-as-judge evals (hallucination/relevance) on local model outputs. License is ELv2 (free internal self-host; just don't resell Phoenix as a service). If you want MIT instead, swap the backend for Langfuse (`docker compose` + Postgres) — OpenLLMetry spans ingest into either, so the instrumentation above is unchanged.

extras.name: nsight-geforce-perfcounter-permission-fix
extras.note: LOAD-BEARING for both Nsight Systems GPU-metrics sampling AND all of Nsight Compute on the GeForce RTX 5090: by default (driver 419.17+) GPU performance-counter access is blocked for non-admin users and the tools fail with ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM. Fix once: NVIDIA Control Panel -> Developer -> Manage GPU Performance Counters -> 'Allow access to the GPU performance counters to all users', then reboot. Alternatively run the profiler from an elevated (Administrator) terminal each time. Without this, every HW-counter read on the consumer card fails — this is the #1 'why doesn't profiling work on my GeForce' gotcha.

extras.name: nvidia-smi-dmon-csv-telemetry-floor
extras.note: The Windows telemetry FLOOR that replaces the (Linux-only) DCGM/dcgm-exporter Prometheus stack on this rig. Zero install — ships with the driver. Stream a 1 Hz timeline of power/util/clocks/mem/temp during any run: `nvidia-smi dmon -s pucm`. research.domain: Attention backends & GPU kernels (Wave 3 deepening) — RTX 5090 / Blackwell sm_120 / Windows 11
research.notes: INSTALL FOR THIS LANE ON THIS RIG (RTX 5090 / sm_120 / 32GB / Win11): For diffusion/video (your actual day-job: Sprite Foundry, ComfyUI SDXL/Flux), the winning stack is SageAttention (already a KB row) via the prebuilt Windows wheel (mobcat40/sageattention-blackwell, sageattention-2.2.0+cu128.torch2.11-cp311 wheel) wired through ComfyUI-KJNodes "Patch Sage Attention" node — NOT the --use-sage-attention flag, NOT pip-installing xformers. SageAttention-3 FP4 (sm_120a) is real and ~1.5-2x over SA2++ on Blackwell FP4 tensor cores, but on Windows it does NOT compile clean from the thu-ml tree without the PR #5 typename/C++ flag patches — budget an afternoon or stay on SA2++ until it stabilizes (recipe: SA3-FP4-5090-Windows-Native). For LLM serving the MLA story is the single most important takeaway of this wave: **FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, TLX Block Attention, and trtllm-gen FMHA all hard-fail on sm_120** because they emit tcgen05/wgmma instructions that exist only on SM100 (datacenter Blackwell) and SM90 (Hopper) — sm_120 (desktop Blackwell) is a THIRD ISA that needs its own kernels nobody has shipped. The ONLY way to run DeepSeek-V3.2/V4 MLA on a 5090 today is FlashInfer's XQA backend (auto-selected on sm_120; recipe: MLA-on-5090-FlashInfer-XQA) — you get ~20 tok/s decode, not FlashMLA's 410 TFLOPS. SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT TAKEAWAY: on the 5090, "Blackwell support" claims are worthless unless they say sm_120 — the high-profile 2026 MLA/sparse kernels (FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, TLX) are all SM100-only; route MLA through FlashInfer-XQA and attention through SageAttention, and never assume a Hopper/B200 kernel will load.

engines.summary: DeepSeek's canonical open-source MLA kernel library and the reference implementation of Multi-head Latent Attention decode/prefill — the kernel behind DeepSeek-V3/V3.2 inference. It ships SM90 (Hopper) and SM100 (datacenter Blackwell, GB200/B200) backends, plus the V3.2 token-sparse 'DeepSeek Sparse Attention' kernels (640/410 TFLOPS). It is genuinely state-of-the-art and MIT-licensed, but it is categorically unavailable on the RTX 5090: sm_120 (desktop Blackwell) is a distinct ISA from sm_100 (datacenter Blackwell), and FlashMLA's matmuls compile only to wgmma (SM90) or tcgen05 (SM100). There is no community sm_120 fork as of 2026-06; vLLM issue #36865 documents it registering as an unsupported target on 5090 source builds. Included here as load-bearing negative intelligence: when you see 'FlashMLA accelerates DeepSeek,' it does NOT mean on your card — route MLA through FlashInfer's XQA backend instead.

engines.summary: Moonshot's CUTLASS kernels for Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), the linear-attention block in Kimi Linear. Requirements are CUDA 12.9+, PyTorch 2.4+, 'SM90 and above'. Its relevance is also narrow: it only matters if you actually serve Kimi-Linear-family models, which is a niche for a single-human game studio. Catalog it as the linear-attention counterpart to FlashMLA; reach for it only if Kimi Linear becomes part of your local LLM crew and you're willing to compile.

engines.summary: DeepSeek's clean, hand-tuned FP8/FP4 GEMM library — the matmul counterpart to FlashMLA and the GEMM engine behind DeepSeek-V3/V4 MoE. The April-2026 'public-release-260416' is a milestone: Mega MoE, FP8xFP4 mixed-precision GEMM, an FP4 Indexer, and a JIT-CPP module that turns it from a kernel library into a runtime. It is MIT-licensed and genuinely best-in-class on Hopper and datacenter Blackwell. But it is the clearest case of the sm_100-vs-sm_120 trap: SM120 shares neither Hopper's wgmma nor SM100's tcgen05.fence, so DeepGEMM's kernels simply have no valid code path on a 5090, and DeepSeek-V4 cannot forward-pass on consumer Blackwell at all until someone writes sm_120 kernels (tracked but unshipped in issues #236/#317). extras.name: SA3-FP4-5090-Windows-Native-build
extras.note: SageAttention-3 FP4 on RTX 5090 (sm_120a), Windows 11 NATIVE. PREREQS (pin exactly): Python 3.13, PyTorch >=2.8.0+cu128 (nightly), CUDA Toolkit 12.8+ (12.8 is the floor for FP4/microscaling PTX; do NOT use 13.x for the rest of your llama.cpp stack per wave-1 finding, but SA3 itself needs 12.8+), VS 2022 Build Tools (MSVC 19.40+), and a CUTLASS checkout. GATING: the SA3 kernels live in the thu-ml/SageAttention repo under sageattention3_blackwell/ — also fill the HuggingFace form at huggingface.co/jt-zhang/SageAttention3 (gated; commercial-use review ~72h). KNOWN WINDOWS BREAKAGE (load-bearing): a clean `python setup.py install` FAILS on Windows/5090 with (1) `cutlass::platform::is_unsigned_v not found` because setup forces /std:c++17 and drops CUTLASS cmake flags, and (2) `error C2061: syntax error: identifier 'LayoutSF'/'SfAtom'` + `C4346 dependent name is not a type` in sageattn/blackwell/kernel_traits.h from a missing `typename`. FIX: apply thu-ml/SageAttention PR #5 (adds the missing `typename` keywords and the CUTLASS flags) BEFORE building; if PR #5 is merged on your checkout you're clean, otherwise cherry-pick it. Manual fallback that unblocks CUTLASS: edit setup.py and bump `-std=c++17` -> `-std=c++20` (CUTLASS 3.x wants C++17 minimum but the 5090 FP4 traits compile cleaner under C++20 with MSVC). BUILD: `git clone https://github.com/thu-ml/SageAttention && cd SageAttention/sageattention3_blackwell && python setup.py install` (after the patch). It compiles two extensions: fp4attn_cuda + fp4quant_cuda, arch=compute_120a,code=sm_120a. HARD CONSTRAINTS of the FP4 kernel: head_dim in {64,128,256} only; NO GQA/MQA (num_heads must == num_heads_k); causal + non-causal both fine; seq rounded internally to multiples of 128. If the native build keeps fighting you, fall back to SA3-prebuilt-wheel-ComfyUI recipe (SA2++ wheel) and revisit when thu-ml ships a Windows-clean SA3.

extras.name: SA3-FP4-5090-Python-API-call
extras.note: Calling SageAttention-3 FP4 once built (RTX 5090 sm_120). The high-level entrypoint mirrors SA2: `from sageattention import sageattn; out = sageattn(q, k, v, tensor_layout='HND', is_causal=False)` — on a Blackwell build this auto-routes Q/K/V through FP4 microscaling. tensor_layout='HND' means [Batch, Heads, Seq, Dim]; use 'NHD' if your tensors are [Batch, Seq, Heads, Dim]. The LOW-LEVEL FP4 kernel signature is `mha_fwd(q,k,v, sfq,sfk,sfv, delta_s, is_causal, per_block_mean, is_bf16)` where q,k are uint8 [B,H,S,D/2] (2 FP4 packed/byte, float_e2m1_t = 1 sign/2 exp/1 mantissa), v is uint8 TRANSPOSED [B,H,D,S/2], and sfq/sfk/sfv are float8_e4m3fn per-block (128-element block) scale factors. Set is_bf16=True to emit BF16 output (recommended for diffusion), False for FP16. per_block_mean=True turns on the delta_s [B,H,S/128,S] FP32 mean-correction (improves accuracy at small cost — turn ON if you see quality loss). ACCURACY POLICY: SA3 FP4 is validated-good on Flux, SD3.5, SDXL, CogVideoX-2B, HunyuanVideo, Mochi — use it freely there. For models that degrade, use the HYBRID strategy: run SA2++ (sageattn_qk_int8_pv_fp8_cuda) at the first/last few denoise steps and SA3 FP4 in the middle. LLMs (Llama/Mistral) are marked experimental for SA3 FP4 — verify per-model, do not assume lossless. Runtime guard: the kernel raises on any non-Blackwell GPU, so a wrong-card import fails loud, not silent.

extras.name: SA3-prebuilt-wheel-ComfyUI-5090-Windows
extras.note: THE PRACTICAL PATH for diffusion/video on the 5090 today (no compiler fights): use the prebuilt SageAttention 2.2.0 / SA2++ Windows wheel, wired via ComfyUI-KJNodes. PIN: this wheel was built against PyTorch 2.11.0.dev20260127 + cu128 + cp311 — your venv MUST match that exact nightly or you rebuild from source. INSTALL (ComfyUI portable): `.\python_embeded\python.exe -m pip install sageattention-2.2.0+cu128.torch2.11-cp311-cp311-win_amd64.whl` (venv: `path\to\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install sageattention-2.2.0+cu128.torch2.11-cp311-cp311-win_amd64.whl`). cu130 wheel also exists (sageattention-2.2.0+cu130.torch2.11-cp311) if you're on cu130 PyTorch — but a cu128 wheel will NOT load on cu130 torch and vice versa. PYTORCH HEADER PATCH (required, MSVC C2872 `::std::string` ambiguity): open `venv\Lib\site-packages\torch\include\torch\csrc\dynamo\compiled_autograd.h` lines ~1135-1136 and comment them out. ENABLE IN COMFYUI (do this, NOT the flag): install ComfyUI-KJNodes, drop the 'Patch Sage Attention' node into the graph BEFORE the sampler, set backend = `sageattn_qk_int8_pv_fp16_cuda`. Do NOT launch ComfyUI with `--use-sage-attention` on the 5090 — it routes to the wrong/unsupported path; the KJNodes patch node is the supported route. MEASURED: ~35% faster diffusion sampling vs SDPA on the 5090. This is your Sprite-Foundry / SDXL-Flux default until SA3 FP4 builds clean on Windows.

extras.name: MLA-on-5090-FlashInfer-XQA-not-FlashMLA
extras.note: Running DeepSeek MLA (V3.2 / V4-Flash) on the RTX 5090 WITHOUT FlashMLA (which can't load on sm_120). FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, and trtllm-gen FMHA are all SM100-only — on sm_120 the trtllm-gen MLA path fails with 'Unsupported architecture' (sglang #24633, TensorRT-LLM #11799: no SM120/SM121 cubins, only SM100/SM103 exist). THE WORKING ROUTE: FlashInfer's MLA support auto-selects the XQA backend on sm_120. Install FlashInfer (>=0.6.2) into your serving env and let auto-backend pick XQA; explicitly avoid forcing the TRTLLM/trtllm-gen MLA prefill backend (it has no sm_120 cubins). In vLLM/SGLang on a 5090, you must also disable FlashMLA targets (vLLM #36865) and NOT rely on SM120 Marlin defaults being correct. MEASURED: DeepSeek-V4-Flash hits ~20+ tok/s decode on a single RTX 5090 via the FlashInfer backend — modest vs FlashMLA's 410 TFLOPS on Hopper, but it actually runs. CAVEAT: NVFP4 mm_fp4 GEMM is reported BROKEN across backends on sm_120 (flashinfer #2577), so prefer BF16/FP8 KV + the XQA decode path over FP4 GEMM for MLA on this card right now. If you only have the 5090, this is the ONLY local MLA option; for heavier DeepSeek serving, 64GB system RAM + ktransformers CPU/GPU offload (kvcache-ai/ktransformers DeepSeek-V4-Flash guide) is the realistic complement.

extras.name: FlashKDA-Kimi-Linear-build-WSL2-sm120-attempt
extras.note: Building FlashKDA for Kimi-Linear-family models — only do this if you actually run Kimi Linear locally. PREREQS: CUDA 12.9+, PyTorch >=2.4, a CUTLASS submodule, C++20 compiler. WINDOWS REALITY: no native build; use WSL2 (Ubuntu) — but remember the wave-2 finding that WSL2 hides FP8/FP4 tensor cores. FlashKDA is bf16-only (no FP4), so WSL2 doesn't cost you FP4 here, but sm_120 is NOT in its tested matrix (H20-only benchmarks). BUILD ATTEMPT: `git clone --recursive https://github.com/MoonshotAI/FlashKDA && cd FlashKDA && FLASH_KDA_CUDA_ARCHS=120a pip install -v --no-build-isolation.` — the default arch list is '90a,100a'; you MUST add/override to include 120a, and there is no guarantee the tcgen05/wgmma-class paths have an sm_120 fallback (expect possible compile failure — this is unverified for the 5090). INTEGRATION (the actual value): with FlashKDA installed, flash-linear-attention auto-routes its `chunk_kda` op to it; opt out with env `FLA_FLASH_KDA=0`. So in practice you `pip install flash-linear-attention` + FlashKDA and your Kimi-Linear inference picks it up transparently. Expected uplift (H20 reference, NOT 5090-measured): 1.72x-2.22x prefill over the FLA baseline. BOTTOM LINE for this rig: low priority — bf16 linear-attention kernel, niche to Kimi models, sm_120 unproven; keep it as a build-from-source experiment, not a default.

extras.name: sm120-vs-sm100-kernel-gate-checklist
extras.note: PRE-FLIGHT before adopting ANY '2026 Blackwell kernel' on the 5090 — paste-this mental checklist (saves hours). (1) GREP the support matrix for the literal string 'sm_120' / '120a' / 'SM120'. If it says only 'Blackwell', 'SM100', '100a', or 'B200' -> it will NOT run on your desktop card. sm_120 (desktop Blackwell, GB202/5090) is a THIRD ISA, distinct from sm_100 (datacenter Blackwell B200/GB200) and sm_90 (Hopper). (2) If the kernel emits `tcgen05.*` (SM100-only) or `wgmma.*` (SM90-only) MMA instructions, it has no valid code path on sm_120 — this is exactly why FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, TLX Block Attention, and trtllm-gen FMHA all fail on the 5090. (3) Confirmed-WORKING on sm_120 today: SageAttention 2.x/2++/3-FP4 (sm_120a kernels), FlashInfer XQA backend (MLA decode), FlexAttention/SDPA (PyTorch cu128), Marlin/Machete (INT4-AWQ GEMM), triton-windows. (4) Confirmed-BROKEN on sm_120 today: FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, TLX Block Attention, trtllm-gen FMHA cubins, FlashInfer NVFP4 mm_fp4 GEMM (#2577). (5) Toolchain pins for sm_120: CUDA 12.8 / cu128 nightly (NOT 13.x for llama.cpp — wave-1 MMQ segfault/5x-slowdown finding), PyTorch cu128 nightly with sm_120 in TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST='12.0', always run CUDA graphs (never eager — ~8x), never `pip install xformers` (use SageAttention). (6) WSL2 vs native: WSL2 hides FP8/FP4 tensor cores -> prefer INT4-AWQ-Marlin in WSL2; do FP4/FP8 work (SA3) on Windows-native.

extras.name: rig-base-cu128-nightly-FIRST (shared prereq for ALL five engines)
extras.note:
Blackwell sm_120 is gated by PyTorch, not by these frameworks. Pin the nightly BEFORE installing any trainer or its setup.py will pull a stable cu12x wheel over your nightly and re-break sm_120. Windows-native (PowerShell): python -m venv E:\AI\venvs\train; E:\AI\venvs\train\Scripts\Activate.ps1 pip install --pre torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu128 python -c "import torch;print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.get_device_capability())" # expect (12,0) == sm_120
Then install the framework with --no-build-isolation so it reuses this torch. NOTE the wave-1/2 rule: pin CUDA 12.8 / cu128 — CUDA 13.x segfaults llama.cpp MMQ and is ~5x slower; do not 'upgrade' to cu130 wheels for the training venv. bitsandbytes for QLoRA needs a sm_120 build — `pip install -U bitsandbytes` then verify `python -m bitsandbytes` reports CUDA 12.8 and no 'no kernel image' error; if it fails, build from source against cu128.

extras.name: ms-swift-install-windows-native (the one to run first on this rig)
extras.note:
On TOP of the cu128-nightly venv above (Windows-native, no WSL2 needed for the transformers backend): pip install -U ms-swift --no-deps # avoid clobbering the nightly torch pip install transformers accelerate datasets peft trl deepspeed # deps explicitly, no torch pip install vllm # the SAME inference engine in this KB — reused for GRPO rollouts
Sanity: `swift sft --help` and `swift rlhf --help` should print. If you see 'sm_120 not compatible', your torch got downgraded — reinstall the nightly and re-run ms-swift with --no-deps. Pin a version for reproducibility: `pip install ms-swift==4.2.3`. Megatron-SWIFT (FP8) is Linux/WSL2 only — stay on the transformers backend for native Windows.

extras.name: ms-swift-qlora-sft-7B-32GB (Qwen3 LoRA, single 5090, Windows-native)
extras.note:
Single-GPU QLoRA SFT that fits 32 GB with room to spare (~700 tok/s class on a 5090). PowerShell: $env:CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='0' swift sft ` --model Qwen/Qwen3-8B ` --train_type lora --quant_bits 4 --quant_method bnb ` --dataset 'AI-ModelScope/alpaca-gpt4-data-en#5000' ` --num_train_epochs 2 --max_length 2048 ` --per_device_train_batch_size 1 --gradient_accumulation_steps 16 ` --gradient_checkpointing true ` --learning_rate 1e-4 --lora_rank 16 --lora_alpha 32 ` --output_dir E:\AI\out\qwen3-8b-lora
If VRAM is tight, drop max_length to 1024 or move to a 4B model. Export merged weights to GGUF for llama.cpp inference: `swift export --adapters E:\AI\out\qwen3-8b-lora\checkpoint-xxx --merge_lora true --to_gguf true` (then quantize/serve with the llama.cpp build from the inference lane). Keeps the train->serve loop entirely on this one rig.

extras.name: ms-swift-grpo-single-gpu-vllm-colocate (RL on ONE 5090)
extras.note:
GRPO RLVR on a single 32 GB card by colocating the vLLM rollout sampler IN the trainer process — the move that makes RL fit on a desktop. Keep the policy small (≤4B) so policy + rollout KV both fit. PowerShell: $env:CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='0'; $env:NPROC_PER_NODE='1' swift rlhf ` --rlhf_type grpo ` --model Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 ` --train_type lora --lora_rank 16 ` --use_vllm true --vllm_mode colocate ` --vllm_gpu_memory_utilization 0.5 ` --dataset 'AI-MO/NuminaMath-TIR#5000' ` --max_completion_length 1024 --num_generations 8 ` --per_device_train_batch_size 1 --gradient_accumulation_steps 8 ` --output_dir E:\AI\out\qwen3-4b-grpo
Tune vllm_gpu_memory_utilization DOWN (0.4-0.5) if you OOM — colocate splits VRAM between the sampler KV-cache and the trainer. GRPO family swap-in: --rlhf_type dapo|gspo|cispo|rloo. Reward functions: built-in for math/format, or pass --reward_funcs for custom verifiable rewards. This is the rig's local alternative to cluster-only OpenRLHF/veRL runs.

extras.name: ms-swift-dpo-preference-tuning (single 5090)
extras.note:
Preference optimization (DPO/KTO/ORPO/SimPO) with LoRA on one card — no separate reward model or rollout needed, so cheaper than GRPO. PowerShell: $env:CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='0' swift rlhf ` --rlhf_type dpo ` --model Qwen/Qwen3-8B ` --train_type lora --quant_bits 4 --quant_method bnb ` --dataset 'AI-ModelScope/hh-rlhf#10000' ` --beta 0.1 --rpo_alpha 1.0 ` --max_length 2048 --per_device_train_batch_size 1 --gradient_accumulation_steps 16 ` --gradient_checkpointing true --learning_rate 5e-6 ` --output_dir E:\AI\out\qwen3-8b-dpo
Swap --rlhf_type to kto / orpo / simpo / cpo for the other preference methods (each has its own loss; KTO needs only binary good/bad labels, handy when you lack paired data). QLoRA (4-bit) keeps an 8B DPO run inside 32 GB.

extras.name: skyrl-wsl2-agentic-rl-setup (research, WSL2 only)
extras.note:
SkyRL is Ray+vLLM Linux-first — run under WSL2 (Ubuntu) on this rig; native Windows is not supported. Inside WSL2 with a cu128 torch: git clone https://github.com/NovaSky-AI/SkyRL && cd SkyRL uv venv && source.venv/bin/activate uv pip install -e skyrl-train # RL trainer (FSDP/Megatron + vLLM rollouts on Ray) uv pip install -e skyrl-gym # tool-use / verifiable-reward task gym uv pip install -e skyrl-agent # async multi-turn agent layer
For local single-GPU experiments use the Tinker-compatible backend (skyrl-tx) rather than the full Ray cluster path. WSL2 WARNING (wave-1/2 rule): FP8/FP4 tensor cores are hidden under WSL2 — train bf16, do NOT expect Blackwell FP8 speedups. Single 32 GB 5090 limits you to ≤4-7B LoRA policies. Use this for long-horizon tool-using agent RL research, not throughput.

extras.name: open-instruct-wsl2-rlvr-reference (study + adapt, WSL2)
extras.note:
Ai2's RLVR/Tülu codebase — Linux+Ray+vLLM, so WSL2 on this rig. The published recipes assume 8 GPUs; on one 5090 lift the recipe and shrink it. Inside WSL2: git clone https://github.com/allenai/open-instruct && cd open-instruct uv sync # pins its own deps incl. cu12x torch+vllm — verify torch.cuda.get_device_capability()==(12,0) after; if a stable wheel landed, force the cu128 nightly back
SFT a small model single-GPU: `python open_instruct/finetune.py --model_name_or_path <small> --use_lora...`. LICENSE CARE: the framework is Apache-2.0 but several Tülu/OLMo recipe datasets are non-commercial/ODC and base models carry community licenses — vet data + base-model license before any commercial fine-tune. Best used to READ how RLVR is wired, then implement the verifiable-reward in ms-swift's --reward_funcs for an actually-single-GPU run.

extras.name: engine-selection-cheatsheet-this-rig
extras.note: Decision tree for the training lane on RTX 5090 / 32 GB / 64 GB RAM / Win11: (1) Plain QLoRA speed, fewest moving parts -> Unsloth (wave 1), ~720 tok/s 7B INT4, Windows-native. (2) SFT/DPO/GRPO across the widest model zoo, single CLI, single-GPU RL via vLLM colocate -> ms-swift (THIS lane's pick), Windows-native. (3) Low-memory full-parameter-style tuning that beats LoRA quality on 32 GB -> LMFlow LISA + ZeRO-3 offload to 64 GB RAM (WSL2). (4) Long-horizon tool-using AGENT RL research -> SkyRL (WSL2). (5) Reading/reproducing frontier RLVR recipes -> open-instruct (WSL2, mind dataset licenses). (6) AVOID NeMo-Aligner for new work — archived 2025-11-19, multi-node only, superseded by NeMo-RL. Universal gotcha: pin cu128 torch nightly FIRST; install every framework with --no-deps/--no-build-isolation so it can't downgrade torch and kill sm_120.
